title: Lower Secondary Science - Kinetic Particle Theory

questions.question: What is the main idea behind the particulate nature of matter?
options: Matter is continuous and smooth with no empty spaces.
Matter is made up of tiny, discrete particles in constant, random motion.
Particles only move when an external force is applied.
Particles in all substances are fixed in rigid rows.
questions.explanation: The particulate model states that all matter consists of tiny discrete particles (atoms, molecules, or ions) that are in continuous, random motion.

questions.question: When smoke particles in air are viewed under a microscope, they move irregularly in random zig-zags. What explains this movement?
options: Tiny, fast-moving air particles collide randomly and unevenly with the smoke particles.
Smoke particles expand and push air particles away.
Air currents blow the smoke particles in fixed circles.
Smoke particles repel each other due to magnetic forces.
questions.explanation: Brownian motion happens because invisible, fast-moving air particles in continuous random motion collide unevenly against the larger smoke particles from all directions.

questions.question: What happens to the particles of a substance when its temperature increases?
options: The particles become larger in size.
The particles move or vibrate faster at higher speeds.
The total number of particles increases.
The particles stop moving and lock together.
questions.explanation: As a substance gets hotter, its particles move or vibrate faster and with greater speed.

questions.question: How does a gas trapped in a closed container exert pressure on the container walls?
options: Gas particles expand and squeeze against the walls.
Gas particles constantly move and collide with the inner walls, exerting a push per unit area.
The weight of stationary gas particles presses against the walls.
Gas particles attract the wall particles strongly.
questions.explanation: Gas particles move randomly at high speeds and continuously hit the inside surfaces of the container, creating an outward push per unit area.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the arrangement and movement of particles in a solid?
options: Closely packed in an orderly arrangement, vibrating about fixed positions.
Closely packed in a disorderly arrangement, sliding past one another.
Far apart in a random arrangement, moving rapidly in all directions.
Spaced far apart with no movement.
questions.explanation: In a solid, strong attractive forces keep particles closely packed in an orderly structure where they can only vibrate about their fixed positions.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the arrangement and movement of particles in a liquid?
options: Arranged in a regular pattern, vibrating about fixed positions.
Closely packed in a disorderly arrangement, sliding past one another.
Very far apart, moving in straight lines at high speeds.
Completely locked in place with large gaps between them.
questions.explanation: In a liquid, particles are closely packed but without regular order, allowing them to slide over and past one another while remaining in contact.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the particles in a gas?
options: Closely packed in regular layers with very strong attractive forces.
Closely packed in random arrangements, sliding over each other.
Very far apart in a random arrangement, moving rapidly in all directions.
Stationary with strong bonds holding them together.
questions.explanation: Gas particles have large spaces between them and very weak attractive forces, moving independently and quickly in all directions.

questions.question: Why can a gas be compressed easily, whereas a solid or a liquid cannot?
options: Gas particles are softer than solid particles.
There are large empty spaces between gas particles, while solid and liquid particles are closely packed.
Gas particles shrink when pushed.
Solid particles disappear under pressure.
questions.explanation: Gas particles are spaced very far apart, so applying pressure pushes them closer together. Particles in solids and liquids are already tightly packed.

questions.question: Why does a solid maintain a fixed shape, whereas a liquid takes the shape of its container?
options: Strong attractive forces hold solid particles in fixed positions, while liquid particles can slide past one another.
Liquid particles have no mass and can flow anywhere.
Solid particles do not move at all.
Liquid particles stick together permanently.
questions.explanation: Solid particles cannot move freely because strong attractive forces lock them into place. Liquid particles can slide around each other, allowing liquids to flow and fill container shapes.

questions.question: What is diffusion?
options: The settling of solid particles to the bottom of a container.
The net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.
The increase in particle size when a substance is heated.
The flow of liquid through a pipe under gravity.
questions.explanation: Diffusion is the overall net movement of particles from an area with more solute particles per unit volume to an area with fewer solute particles per unit volume.

questions.question: Why do gases diffuse more readily than liquids, while diffusion does not occur readily in solids?
options: Gas particles move faster and have larger spaces between them, whereas solid particles are held tightly in fixed positions.
Liquid particles repel each other and cannot mix.
Solid particles are too large to move.
Gas particles are pulled by gravity more strongly.
questions.explanation: Gas particles move at very high speeds through large spaces between particles. In solids, particles can only vibrate in place and cannot travel across the material.

questions.question: A drop of food colouring is placed into hot water and cold water without stirring. Why does the colour spread more readily in hot water?
options: Water particles move faster at higher temperatures, causing more frequent collisions and faster mixing.
Hot water dissolves the food colouring into separate chemical elements.
The food colouring particles become lighter in hot water.
Cold water particles push the food colouring down to the bottom.
questions.explanation: Higher temperatures make the water and colouring particles move faster, leading to quicker mixing and a faster rate of diffusion.

questions.question: In a sealed glass tube, cotton wool soaked in ammonia gas (lighter) and hydrochloric acid (heavier) are placed at opposite ends. Where does the white ring of ammonium chloride form?
options: Exactly in the center of the tube.
Closer to the hydrochloric acid end because the lighter ammonia particles move faster and diffuse more readily.
Closer to the ammonia end because heavier particles travel faster.
At both ends of the tube without meeting.
questions.explanation: Lighter gas particles travel at higher speeds than heavier gas particles, so ammonia travels farther along the tube before reacting with hydrogen chloride.

questions.question: When two gases in a closed jar become completely and uniformly mixed, what happens to the movement of the individual particles?
options: The particles stop moving completely.
The particles continue moving randomly in all directions at their normal speeds.
The particles slow down and settle at the bottom.
The particles form permanent bonds and lock in place.
questions.explanation: Even after mixing is complete and net diffusion becomes zero, individual particles never stop and continue moving randomly in all directions.

questions.question: A crystal of purple potassium manganate(VII) is placed at the bottom of a beaker of water. Over time, the purple colour spreads throughout the water without stirring. Why does this happen?
options: The crystal reacts with water to produce air bubbles that carry the colour up.
Particles from the crystal dissolve and move randomly into the spaces between water particles from higher to lower concentration.
Water particles pull the crystal upward in one large clump.
Gravity forces the purple particles to float on top of the water.
questions.explanation: As the crystal dissolves, individual purple particles move randomly through the gaps between water particles, spreading from where they are concentrated to where there are fewer.

questions.question: When an iron rod is heated, it expands. What happens to its particles during expansion?
options: The individual particles become larger in size.
The particles vibrate faster and push each other slightly further apart.
New iron particles are created inside the rod.
The attractive forces between particles disappear completely.
questions.explanation: Heating causes the particles to vibrate faster and more vigorously, increasing the average distance between neighboring particles.

questions.question: When a metal ball undergoes thermal expansion, what happens to the size and mass of each individual particle?
options: Particle size increases, but mass remains unchanged.
Both particle size and mass increase.
Both particle size and mass remain unchanged.
Particle mass increases, but size remains unchanged.
questions.explanation: Individual particles themselves do not grow, shrink, gain mass, or lose mass. Expansion is caused solely by an increase in the space between the particles.

questions.question: A sample of gas is sealed inside a rigid metal tank and cooled from 80°C to 20°C. What happens to its mass?
options: Mass decreases because the particles move more slowly.
Mass remains constant because the number of particles does not change.
Mass increases because the gas particles become more dense.
Mass decreases because particles escape through the metal walls.
questions.explanation: Mass is conserved because no particles enter or leave the sealed tank. Cooling only makes the particles move more slowly.

questions.question: When a liquid in a beaker is heated, its volume expands while its mass is conserved. How does its density change?
options: Density increases because particles become heavier.
Density decreases because the same mass of particles occupies a larger volume.
Density remains unchanged because mass and volume change equally.
Density increases because particles are pushed closer together.
questions.explanation: Density equals mass divided by volume. Since the number of particles (mass) stays the same while the space between them increases (volume increases), density decreases.

questions.question: When a heated copper block cools down and contracts, what happens at the particulate level?
options: The particles vibrate more slowly and move closer together, while total mass is conserved.
The particles shrink in individual size, reducing the total mass.
Particles leave the copper block, causing it to lose weight.
The particles stop vibrating and fuse together.
questions.explanation: During cooling, particles vibrate more slowly and the spaces between them decrease, causing the total volume to shrink while total mass remains unchanged.

questions.question: What happens to the arrangement and movement of particles when ice melts into water?
options: Particles vibrate fast enough to break out of their fixed positions and begin sliding past one another.
Particles move farther apart and become completely stationary.
Particles split into individual hydrogen and oxygen atoms.
Particles form a more orderly lattice with smaller spaces.
questions.explanation: During melting, particles vibrate fast enough to overcome the fixed positions of the solid structure, breaking down into a disorderly arrangement where they slide over each other.

questions.question: Why does the temperature of a pure solid remain constant while it is melting, even though heating continues?
options: The heat supplied is used to overcome the attractive forces holding particles in fixed positions rather than increasing their speed.
The substance stops absorbing heat from the burner.
The particles lose their motion completely during the state change.
Heat is lost instantly to the surroundings as soon as melting begins.
questions.explanation: During a change of state, the heat supplied is used to overcome the forces of attraction between particles to change their arrangement, so particle speed and temperature remain constant.

questions.question: What is the difference between boiling and evaporation in terms of where the state change occurs?
options: Evaporation occurs throughout the entire liquid, while boiling occurs only at the surface.
Evaporation occurs only at the liquid surface below the boiling point, while boiling occurs throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature.
Evaporation involves chemical reactions, while boiling is purely physical.
Evaporation occurs at a fixed temperature, while boiling occurs at any temperature.
questions.explanation: Evaporation is a surface process that can happen at temperatures below the boiling point, whereas boiling takes place throughout the entire bulk of the liquid at its fixed boiling temperature.

questions.question: What happens to particles during boiling when a liquid changes into a gas?
options: Particles move fast enough to completely overcome the attractive forces between them and spread far apart.
Particles expand in size until they burst into vapor.
Particles slow down and pack into rigid layers.
Particles lose their mass and float away.
questions.explanation: During boiling, particles move rapidly and completely overcome the attractive forces holding them in the liquid state, moving far apart as gas particles.
